Thought: Interim report; primary O1 outcome and all human results pending by design. Strong provenance/pre-registration/honesty; main claims about accuracy unsupported yet. Gatekeeper rate vs pilot human 6% gap is a central tension. Same-family judge, low recall, access-bound coverage, single-author-team framing.
Summary: GP-RareLink builds per-person GA4GH Phenopacket records from open-access rare-disease case reports using a frozen SLIDERS-style Claude pipeline with verbatim quotes, three-state phenotypes and a Claude gatekeeper, scored against held-out ClinVar and OMIM. Across six registered diseases (350 papers, 2,836 phenopackets) all values have verbatim spans, the gatekeeper flags 0.43% unsupported, HGVS recall against ClinVar is low (10-35%), OMIM recovery is 57%, and 214 gap candidates await adjudication. The primary human audit, calibration, adjudication and bias results are pending; two pilot audits found 6.0% and 6.3% unsupported.
Strengths: Provenance-first design with deterministic span checks and a pre-registered, frozen pipeline; deviations are logged and the ground-truth isolation is tested.
Exceptional honesty: gatekeeper share is explicitly not an error rate, pilot audits missing the 2% target are reported, negative and unfavorable findings are foregrounded.
Careful statistics: exact intervals, operating characteristics of rule C (P(pass) at true rates, upper bounds), publication-cluster bootstrap, pre-fixed calibration floor.
Held-out evaluation design with OMIM and ClinVar dated snapshots, tiered HGVS matching, and clear diagnosis that recall is limited by citation, conversion and access rather than reading.
Broad scope (twelve diseases, open-weight comparison, memorization probe) with clear separation of registered versus exploratory results.
Weaknesses: The central claim (accuracy a person can demonstrate, <2% unsupported) is untested: the only human audits (pilot, one rater each, earlier pipeline) found ~6%, and the gatekeeper caught only 2 of 6 and 1 of 4 of those errors. The headline 0.43% is therefore close to uninformative about true error, and a Claude judge of Claude output may share blind spots.

Recall and coverage are weak and mostly unresolved: HGVS recall 10-35% at tier 1, only 28% of corpus papers have open full text (Tangier 14%), so the gap count is a lower bound and OMIM recovery (57%) is driven by access; misses are untriaged, so concordance cannot yet be interpreted as accuracy or precision (overlap is explicitly not precision).

Evidence for the downstream deliverables is thin: no candidate is adjudicated, no bias deviation computed, expert-minutes undefined, the open-weight comparison has no human audit and uses a Claude judge; HA20 is a development disease and ClinVar-seeded; deduplication is acknowledged weak (6 of 93 false merges in pilot, 9 of 38 repeat papers differ, 19 unmerged groups). Methodological complexity and a very dense, appendix-dependent presentation make it hard to follow; the self-authorship by Claude Code limits independence.
Questions: How will you handle the gatekeeper's low sensitivity (2 of 6) when interpreting audit results, and can a human-labelled subset of removed claims estimate false negatives?
Can you give recall against ClinVar restricted to papers with open full text and non-curation citations to separate extraction failure from citation artifacts?
What is the plan if the primary audit fails rule C, and which frozen gaps (hedging, relative attribution) will be reported as a deviation versus redesign?
How do inter-rater agreement and calibration floor results change the registered-rater selection without introducing bias?
Limitations: No human-rated accuracy for the frozen pipeline; gatekeeper is a same-family model judge.
Open-access-only corpus bounds recall and gap counts.
Deduplication, notation and isoform placement artefacts; HA20 development bias.
Licensing and history exposure of transcripts unresolved; costs are estimates.
